catalog.label: Base
catalog.description: Baseline security controls for PAN-OS firewalls.

controls.name: Disable Telnet on Management Surfaces
controls.description: Telnet transmits credentials and session content in cleartext. It must remain disabled; SSH is the only acceptable CLI transport. Every management surface - MGT, Aux-1, Aux-2, and any layer-3 interface carrying an interface-management-profile - is assessed, because the risk is the same wherever the service is exposed.
controls.rationale: Telnet exposes administrator credentials and session content to anyone able to observe the path, and a management surface is by definition reachable by administrators.
controls.audit: Review each management surface and verify Telnet is not enabled. Telnet is disabled by default on current releases, so a finding means it was deliberately re-enabled.
controls.remediation: Disable Telnet on the surface reporting it and use SSH instead.

controls.name: Disable HTTP on Management Surfaces
controls.description: Unencrypted HTTP management exposes credentials and session tokens. HTTPS must be used instead. Every management surface - MGT, Aux-1, Aux-2, and any layer-3 interface carrying an interface-management-profile - is assessed, because the risk is the same wherever the service is exposed.
controls.rationale: HTTP management carries administrator credentials and session cookies in cleartext, and offers no assurance that the device being managed is the intended one.
controls.audit: Review each management surface and verify HTTP is not enabled. HTTP is disabled by default, so a finding means it was deliberately re-enabled.
controls.remediation: Disable HTTP on the surface reporting it and use HTTPS instead.

controls.name: Restrict Management Access to Permitted IP Addresses
controls.description: Limits which source addresses may reach a management surface. A surface with no permitted-source list accepts any host that can route to it. Every management surface - MGT, Aux-1, Aux-2, and any layer-3 interface carrying an interface-management-profile - is assessed, because the risk is the same wherever the service is exposed.
controls.rationale: Restricting permitted IP addresses reduces exposure of the management plane and limits administrative access attempts to trusted networks or jump hosts.
controls.audit: Review each surface's permitted-source list and verify only approved administrative networks or hosts appear. An absent or empty list means unrestricted.
controls.remediation: Configure permitted IP addresses using approved management subnets or jump-host addresses. Avoid broad ranges unless explicitly justified.

controls.name: Administrative Services on Data-Plane Interfaces
controls.description:
Every data-plane interface with an administrative service enabled is reported, so that those facing untrusted networks can be identified. Management on a data-plane interface bypasses the management-plane isolation model.

This control enumerates rather than judges. Whether an interface faces an untrusted network cannot be determined from configuration - a zone name carries no trust semantics the device enforces - so the finding states a fact and the assessor decides. Only the five administrative services raise a finding; ping, response pages, HTTP-OCSP and the User-ID listeners are reachability and service functions and are reported as context.
controls.rationale: An administrative service on a data-plane interface is reachable from whatever that interface faces, which may include untrusted or Internet-facing networks. The management-plane isolation model assumes administration arrives on the management plane.
controls.audit: Review each reported interface. Confirm the interface does not face an untrusted network, or that the exposure is operationally required and restricted by a permitted-source list.
controls.remediation: Remove the interface management profile, or reduce it to the services actually required and bind a permitted-source list.

controls.name: Ensure firewall rules are not overly permissive
controls.description: Firewall security policy rules should be configured to allow only the minimum required access necessary for the intended traffic flow. Rules should avoid overly broad source, destination, user, application, service, or action criteria, including unnecessary use of any, broad network ranges, unrestricted services, or excessive application allowances.
controls.rationale: Overly permissive firewall rules increase the attack surface by allowing unnecessary network access and reducing the effectiveness of segmentation and least-privilege enforcement.
controls.audit: Review allowed firewall security policy rules and identify rules with broad or unrestricted match criteria, including any sources, destinations, users, applications, or services, broad address objects, broad service groups, or allow actions that exceed the documented technical requirement.
controls.remediation: Modify overly permissive rules to restrict access to the minimum required sources, destinations, users, applications, and services. Remove unused broad rules or replace them with more specific rules aligned to the intended traffic flow.

controls.name: Ensure High Availability is enabled where required
controls.description: High Availability should be enabled on firewalls that are expected to operate as part of a redundant firewall pair.
controls.rationale: Firewalls that enforce critical network paths can become single points of failure if High Availability is not configured. Enabling HA supports service continuity during device failure, maintenance, or controlled failover events.
controls.audit: Review the High Availability configuration and verify that HA is enabled for firewalls that require redundant operation.
controls.remediation: Configure High Availability on the firewall pair, including HA interfaces, peer settings, HA group settings, synchronization settings, and failover monitoring appropriate to the deployment.

controls.name: Ensure High Availability session synchronization is enabled
controls.description: High Availability state synchronization should be enabled for HA firewall pairs where session preservation is required during failover.
controls.rationale: Without session synchronization, active sessions may be dropped during failover, which can disrupt business applications, user access, VPN traffic, and long-lived connections.
controls.audit: Review the HA state synchronization setting and verify that state synchronization is enabled on both HA peers where session preservation is required.
controls.remediation: Enable HA state synchronization and verify HA2 connectivity between peers. Confirm that both peers have consistent state synchronization settings.

controls.name: Ensure High Availability link monitoring is enabled where required
controls.description: High Availability link monitoring should be enabled for critical dataplane interfaces or interface groups where link failure should trigger HA failover.
controls.rationale: If link monitoring is not configured, a firewall may remain active even when critical dataplane links have failed, causing traffic disruption without triggering failover to the peer device.
controls.audit: Review the HA monitoring configuration and verify that link monitoring is enabled for critical interfaces or interface groups.
controls.remediation: Enable HA link monitoring and define monitored link groups for critical interfaces. Configure the failure condition according to the redundancy design.

controls.name: Ensure a login banner is configured
controls.description: A login banner should be configured to notify users that access is restricted to authorized users and that activity may be monitored.
controls.rationale: A login banner supports administrative accountability and provides legal or policy notice before access to the firewall management interface.
controls.audit: Review the system login banner configuration and verify that a non-empty approved login banner is configured.
controls.remediation: Configure an approved login banner that states authorized-use restrictions and monitoring expectations consistent with organizational policy.

controls.name: Ensure the device management idle timeout is less than or equal to 10 minutes
controls.description: The device management idle timeout should be configured to automatically close inactive administrative sessions after 10 minutes or less.
controls.rationale: Inactive administrative sessions can be misused if an administrator leaves a workstation unattended. A short idle timeout reduces the opportunity for unauthorized use of an existing management session.
controls.audit: Review the management authentication settings and verify that the idle timeout is configured to 10 minutes or less and is not set to never timeout.
controls.remediation: Configure the management idle timeout to 10 minutes or less.

controls.name: Ensure redundant NTP servers are configured
controls.description: The firewall should be configured with primary and secondary NTP servers.
controls.rationale: Accurate and consistent time is required for reliable log correlation, event investigation, certificate validation, authentication, and forensic analysis. Redundant NTP servers reduce the risk of time drift if one time source is unavailable.
controls.audit: Review the device service settings and verify that both primary and secondary NTP servers are configured.
controls.remediation: Configure approved primary and secondary NTP servers for the firewall. Use internal enterprise NTP sources where available.
